title: Thyroid – Hypothyroidism: Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Daily Routine
excerpt: Tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, hair fall and constipation — these are common symptoms of hypothyroidism (low thyroid hormone). Learn the causes from an Ayurvedic view, the necessary tests, the right way to take thyroid medicine, what to eat and avoid, yoga-pranayama, safe home remedies and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“I feel tired all the time, my weight keeps increasing, my hair is falling” — behind such complaints there is often low thyroid (hypothyroidism). This problem is very common in India, and is found many times more often in women than in men.

The good news is that a simple blood test detects it, and with the right medicine, diet and routine most people live a normal life. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What is the thyroid and hypothyroidism?

The thyroid is a small butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It makes hormones called T3 and T4, which set the body's “speed” — making energy from food, heartbeat, body temperature, digestion, mental alertness and, in women, the menstrual cycle.

When the thyroid cannot make enough hormone, the whole working of the body slows down — this is called hypothyroidism. Its most common cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, in which the body's own immune system damages the thyroid. Iodine deficiency, thyroid surgery or radio-iodine treatment, some medicines and inflammation after childbirth can also be causes. Remember, hyperthyroidism (excess hormone) is a different disease, with a different treatment.

The Ayurvedic view

Ayurvedic texts have no disease named “thyroid”, but its symptoms are understood as weakness of Agni (especially Dhatvagni), imbalance of Kapha and Vata, and increase of Meda dhatu. Weak Agni produces ama (undigested residue) in the body, Kapha symptoms like heaviness, sluggishness and swelling increase, and Vata causes dryness, constipation and hair fall. Swelling of the gland in the neck (goitre) is called Galaganda in Ayurveda:

निबद्धः श्वयथुर्यस्य मुष्कवल्लम्बते गले ।
महान् वा यदि वा ह्रस्वो गलगण्डं तमादिशेत् ॥
— Sushruta Samhita, Nidana Sthana 11

Meaning: When a person has a fixed (bound) swelling in the neck that hangs like a scrotum — whether large or small — it should be called Galaganda. In today's language this is enlargement of the thyroid gland (goitre).

That is why the basis of care in Ayurveda is — correcting Agni, keeping Kapha and Meda balanced, regular exercise and a cheerful mind — and all of this alongside modern tests and necessary medicines.

Main causes and risks

  • Being a woman, especially after 30, in pregnancy, after childbirth and around menopause
  • Someone in the family having thyroid disease
  • Other autoimmune diseases — such as type 1 diabetes, vitiligo (white patches), rheumatoid arthritis
  • Iodine deficiency (not using iodised salt)
  • Thyroid or neck surgery, radiation to the neck, radio-iodine treatment
  • Some medicines, such as lithium or amiodarone
  • According to Ayurveda — sleeping in the day, no exercise, heavy-cold-sweet food and long mental stress, which weaken Agni and increase Kapha

Symptoms

  • Tiredness all the time, sluggishness and excess sleep
  • Weight gain without eating more, swelling of the face and around the eyes
  • Feeling colder than others
  • Constipation, dry skin, hair fall and brittle nails
  • Low mood, poor concentration, forgetfulness
  • In women, irregular or heavy periods, difficulty in conceiving
  • Muscle pain and cramps, hoarse voice, slow heartbeat
  • Raised cholesterol; sometimes swelling in the neck (goitre)

Tests

Thyroid disease cannot be confirmed by symptoms alone — a blood test is essential:

  • TSH — the most important test; it is raised in hypothyroidism
  • Free T4 (sometimes T3) — the actual hormone level
  • Anti-TPO antibodies — to detect Hashimoto's (autoimmune cause); if there is a lump in the neck, the doctor may also advise an ultrasound

Thyroid testing is especially important for women planning pregnancy or who are pregnant, because the mother's thyroid affects the development of the baby's brain. About 6–8 weeks after starting medicine or changing its dose, the doctor rechecks TSH.

The right way to take thyroid medicine

Most patients are given levothyroxine (thyroid hormone tablet) by the doctor. To get its full benefit:

  • Take the tablet every morning on an empty stomach with plain water, and do not take tea, milk or breakfast for 30–60 minutes after it
  • Take calcium or iron tablets, antacids and soy products at least 4 hours apart from the tablet
  • Take it at the same time and in the same way every day; do not keep changing brands
  • Do not stop the tablet on your own even if you feel well — only the doctor should change the dose after seeing the TSH report

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

The aim of diet is — to kindle Agni, reduce Kapha and heaviness, and give the body all the necessary nutrients.

What to eat

  • Iodised salt — in normal amounts (no extra salt on top)
  • Grains: barley, bajra, jowar, ragi, old rice, daliya
  • Pulses: moong, masoor, kulthi (horse gram) — with mild spices
  • Vegetables: bottle gourd, ridge gourd, pointed gourd, pumpkin, drumstick, spinach, fenugreek leaves, carrot — cooked
  • Fruits: apple, pomegranate, papaya, guava, amla
  • Seeds: flaxseed, pumpkin and sunflower seeds — in small amounts
  • Spices: dry ginger, black pepper, cumin, turmeric, cinnamon — for digestion; lukewarm water

What to avoid or greatly reduce

  • Maida, bakery items, sweets, too much sugar and packaged food
  • Fried, very heavy, cold and stale food
  • Cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli in very large amounts and raw — cooked and in normal amounts is fine
  • Soybean and soy products — especially around the time of the tablet
  • Tea or coffee immediately after the medicine
  • Extra iodine or kelp tablets without a Vaidya's/doctor's advice — too much iodine is also harmful

Daily routine, yoga and pranayama

  • Wake up before sunrise; do not sleep during the day
  • Walk briskly or do light exercise for 30–45 minutes daily
  • Eat at fixed times and only when hungry; keep dinner light
  • Sleep 7–8 hours daily and meditate to reduce stress
  • Control weight gradually and regularly

Yoga and pranayama

  • Asanas: Surya Namaskar (at a slow pace), Bhujangasana, Setu Bandhasana, Matsyasana, Ustrasana, Pawanmuktasana
  • Pranayama: Ujjayi, Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari; Kapalbhati only after learning it, and with caution

Do neck-pressure poses like Sarvangasana, Halasana and Matsyasana only under a trained teacher's supervision; avoid them if you have cervical (neck) problems, high BP, heart disease, eye problems or pregnancy. Do not do Kapalbhati in high BP, heart disease, hernia or pregnancy.

Safe home remedies

  • Dry ginger and lukewarm water: dry ginger or fresh ginger in food, lukewarm water through the day — for digestion
  • Coriander water: soak whole coriander seeds overnight, strain and drink in the morning (1 hour after the thyroid tablet)
  • Amla: fresh amla or amla juice — rich in vitamin C
  • Flaxseed: a little roasted flaxseed — helpful in constipation
  • For dry skin: gentle massage with sesame oil before bathing

These remedies are only supportive — they do not make up for the lack of thyroid hormone. Always keep the gap mentioned above between the thyroid tablet and food or home drinks.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for Galaganda, weak Agni and increased Meda, such as Kanchanar (classical formulations like Kanchanar Guggulu), Guggulu, Ashwagandha, Punarnava, Trikatu (dry ginger-black pepper-long pepper) and Brahmi. However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age, TSH report and current medicines.
  • Never stop or reduce your thyroid tablet (levothyroxine) on your own. Ayurvedic treatment can run alongside, but the dose of the medicine should be changed only by the doctor after seeing the TSH report.
  • Some herbs like Ashwagandha can change thyroid hormone levels — get TSH rechecked after starting them; they can be harmful in hyperthyroidism (excess hormone). Take herbs at least 4 hours apart from the thyroid tablet.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any medicine only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “thyroid removed from the root” or “you will be off the tablet forever”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Extreme drowsiness, confusion, near-unconsciousness, the body becoming very cold or slow breathing — go to hospital immediately
  • Rapidly increasing swelling or a hard lump in the neck, difficulty in swallowing or breathing, a persistent change in voice
  • Fast heartbeat, chest pain, excess sweating, tremors or anxiety after starting the medicine or increasing the dose
  • Thyroid disease found in pregnancy — see the doctor immediately, as the dose often needs to be changed
  • In a newborn, excess sleepiness, poor feeding, prolonged jaundice or constipation — ask about a thyroid test after birth

Summary — points to remember

  • If you have tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold and hair fall, get a TSH test
  • Thyroid tablet in the morning on an empty stomach, at the same time daily; do not stop it on your own
  • Iodised salt, light-warm-fresh food; less maida, sugar and fried food
  • Daily exercise, yoga, good sleep; do not sleep in the day
  • TSH test every 6–12 months (or as advised by the doctor); Ayurvedic treatment only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya
